Save a plot with publication-ready defaults

Source: R/reporting.R
save_plot.Rd

A convenience wrapper around ggplot2::ggsave() with sensible defaults for figures in papers and reports: a moderate size, 300 dpi, and the output directory created if needed. The device is inferred from the file extension, and PDF, EPS and TIFF files are written to pass the technical checks journals run on submitted figures.

Usage

save_plot(
  filename,
  plot = ggplot2::last_plot(),
  width = 7,
  height = 4.5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  ...
)

Arguments

filename

Output file path. The extension sets the device (e.g. .png, .pdf, .eps, .tiff).

plot

The plot to save; defaults to the last plot drawn.

width, height

Dimensions.

units

Units for width and height.

dpi

Resolution for raster devices. An EPS rasterises its translucent layers, and whatever they overlap, at this resolution or at 600 dpi, whichever is higher.

...

Passed to ggplot2::ggsave(), which passes what it does not use on to the device. A device or device argument given here overrides the defaults described under "Formats journals accept".

Value

The filename, invisibly.

Formats journals accept

When no device is given, three formats are written differently from ggplot2's defaults.

A PDF is written with grDevices::cairo_pdf(), which embeds its fonts. ggplot2's default, grDevices::pdf(), names the fonts without embedding them.

An EPS or PostScript file is written with grDevices::cairo_ps(), with its fonts embedded too. PostScript has no transparency, and grDevices::postscript() leaves every translucent layer out of the file: the points and the confidence band of the plot in the examples below vanish. cairo_ps() rasterises those layers, together with whatever they overlap, at fallback_resolution, by default max(dpi, 600) here. A message says so when a layer of the plot, or of any panel of a patchwork, is translucent. A PDF keeps such layers as vector graphics.

A TIFF is compressed with LZW, which is lossless. Uncompressed, a figure of 7 by 4.5 inches at 300 dpi takes 8.1 MiB, and one at the largest size PLOS accepts takes more than the 10 MB PLOS allows. The TIFF is drawn on white unless bg is given, so a transparent background, as in ggplot2::theme_void(), leaves no alpha channel in the file.

Without cairo, a PDF is written with pdf() and a message says how to embed its fonts with grDevices::embedFonts(), and an EPS is written with postscript() and a warning. R for macOS from CRAN loads cairo only where XQuartz (https://www.xquartz.org) is installed, and a Mac with neither XQuartz nor ragg writes the TIFF uncompressed, with a warning from grDevices::tiff(). A device, or a device argument such as fallback_resolution, compression or bg, passed in ... is used as given, so device = "pdf", device = "eps" or device = "tiff" restores ggplot2's own behaviour.

Which formats three publishers accepted on 2 October 2026:

FormatPLOSNature (final artwork)Elsevier
PDFNoYes, as vector artYes
EPSYes, with fonts embeddedYes, as vector artYes, with fonts embedded
TIFFYes, LZW-compressed RGB or greyscale, no alpha channel, at most 10 MBNoYes

Nature also asks for fonts embedded as TrueType 2 or 42, never Type 3, and for line art and text that are not rasterised. A figure with translucent layers therefore goes to Nature as a PDF. Elsevier asks for a graph sent as a TIFF at 1000 dpi, so pass dpi = 1000 for one.

The Python twin takes the plot first, as save_plot(plot, filename).

References

PLOS ONE. Figures. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/s/figures

Nature. Guide to preparing final artwork. https://www.nature.com/documents/nature-final-artwork.pdf

Nature research figure guide. Preparing figures: our specifications. https://research-figure-guide.nature.com/figures/preparing-figures-our-specifications/

Elsevier. Artwork overview. https://www.elsevier.com/about/policies-and-standards/author/artwork-and-media-instructions/artwork-overview

Examples

p <- scatter_trend(crop_yield, fertiliser, yield)
tmp <- file.path(tempdir(), "yield.png")
save_plot(tmp, p)

# A TIFF well within the 10 MB that PLOS allows.
save_plot(file.path(tempdir(), "yield.tiff"), p)
